papers.abstract: Dysnatremia is common in critically ill patients and has been linked to poor outcomes and renal prognosis. Burn patients are particularly vulnerable, but the prognostic significance of dysnatremia in this population remains unclear. We conducted a single-center retrospective cohort study of 1,758 burn patients admitted to a French burn center between 2011 and 2023. Dysnatremia was defined as at least one episode of hyponatremia ( 145 mmol/L) during intensive care unit (ICU) stay. The primary endpoint was the incidence of dysnatremia; secondary endpoints included major adverse kidney events (MAKE) at ICU discharge and acute kidney injury (AKI) occurrence and severity. Dysnatremia occurred in 56.3% of patients (n = 990), with hyponatremia in 50.5% (n = 888) and hypernatremia in 23.8% (n = 418). MAKE at ICU discharge did not differ between hyponatremic and normonatremic patients (12.6% vs. 10.9%, p = 0.304) but was sixfold higher with hypernatremia (32.3% vs. 5.4%, p < 0.001). After adjustment for age and burned total body surface area, hypernatremia was independently associated with MAKE at ICU discharge (adjusted hazard ratio [aHR] 4.03; 95% confidence interval [CI]: 2.92-5.56; p < 0.001), whereas hyponatremia was not (aHR 1.15; 95% CI: 0.85-1.55; p = 0.377). Clustering analysis identified three phenotypes: Cluster B (severe burns, worst outcomes), Cluster A (older patients, mostly hyponatremic, intermediate outcomes), and Cluster C (younger patients, mild burns, best outcomes). Dysnatremia affects over half of burn patients. Sodium disturbances should be viewed as markers of systemic severity, warranting close monitoring and preventive strategies.

papers.abstract: Fluid accumulation in surgical patients is associated with worse outcomes. Lung ultrasound (LUS) and venous excess ultrasound (VExUS) grading can assess congestion and thereby fluid tolerance. However, evidence regarding epidemiology, feasibility, and associations of reduced fluid tolerance with outcomes in surgical patients is lacking. This was a prospective single-centre observational cohort study in patients undergoing major gastrointestinal surgery. LUS and VExUS were performed before surgery and daily for up to 5 days after surgery. Reduced fluid tolerance was defined as pulmonary congestion (B profile on LUS), systemic congestion (VExUS ≥2), or both. The primary outcome was the prevalence of reduced fluid tolerance. Secondary outcomes were feasibility of ultrasound assessments, Clavien-Dindo grade ≥3 complications, and length of stay (LOS). Of the 200 participants included, 73 (37%) exhibited signs of reduced fluid tolerance, most commonly on postoperative day 4 (n=28; 14%). Reduced fluid tolerance was primarily driven by pulmonary congestion (n=69; 95%), whereas systemic congestion was rare. In most affected patients (47 of 73; 64%), reduced fluid tolerance was limited to 1 day. Of 1200 planned assessments, 146 (12%) were missing: 123 because participants declined, mostly owing to the burden of repeated assessments, and 23 (2%) because of incomplete views. Reduced fluid tolerance was associated with LOS of >7 days (odds ratio 3.29; 95% CI 1.03-10.70), but not with major postoperative complications (hazard ratio 1.18; 95% CI 0.49-2.86). Reduced fluid tolerance detected by ultrasound is common after major gastrointestinal surgery and associated with increased LOS. Ultrasound assessments were technically feasible, but repeated assessments were perceived as a burden by a substantial proportion of patients. NCT06166719 (principal investigator: A.P.J. Vlaar; first registered: 04-12-2023).

papers.abstract: Cells resist viral infection by triggering rapid and sensitive innate immune responses, initiated by cytoplasmic viral sensor proteins (CyVSP), retinoic acid-inducible gene I (RIG-I), melanoma differentiation-associated protein 5 (MDA-5), and protein kinase R (PKR). Our single-cell analysis reveals that viral replication requires a supra-unitary viral genome input, significantly more than one, which we define as the virion input threshold for replication (VITREP). This threshold varies depending on viruses and cell types, independently of viral protein synthesis. Through mathematical modeling and experimental testing, we uncover that supra-unitary viral genome quantities activate negative feedback regulators (NFR) of CyVSP, including death-associated protein kinase 1 (DAPK1), Rio kinase 3 (RIOK3), and protein phosphatase 2 regulatory subunit alpha (PPP2R2A), that suppress innate immune responses and allow replication. We validate key predictions of our model, namely that downregulating NFR reduces replication, whereas upregulating NFR or coinfecting cells promotes replication. Together, these findings reveal a fundamental mechanism governing viral infectivity and tissue tropism.

papers.abstract: To determine whether injection pressure and pressure-time characteristics can discriminate potentially hazardous needle-tip locations during peripheral nerve injection. Systematic review of experimental preclinical studies with narrative synthesis. Animal, ex vivo biological nerve, and human cadaver models of peripheral nerve injection. Needle placement and injection at intraneural, intrafascicular, perineural, or extraneural locations. CENTRAL, PubMed, Embase, and Web of Science were searched from inception to April 28, 2026 and updated on September 19, 2026. Studies reporting opening, peak, or plateau pressure or pressure-time characteristics in relation to anatomically defined needle-tip location were eligible. Human clinical studies and non-biological bench models were excluded. Risk of bias was evaluated using SYRCLE for animal studies and a domain-based framework for cadaveric studies. Because of substantial heterogeneity in experimental models, injection techniques, and pressure definitions, meta-analysis was not considered appropriate. Twenty-eight studies met the inclusion criteria: 12 animal or animal ex vivo studies and 16 human cadaver studies. Intraneural injection was generally associated with higher peak and plateau pressures than perineural injection, but substantial overlap occurred across needle locations. Importantly, low pressure did not reliably rule out intraneural injection, while elevated pressure was also observed during needle-nerve contact and fascial injection. Consequently, the commonly proposed 15-psi threshold showed inconsistent sensitivity across experimental settings. Lower thresholds, including 12 psi, appeared more sensitive in some models but have not been clinically validated. Beyond absolute pressure values, the rate of pressure rise and pressure-time curve morphology showed potential for differentiating needle-tip locations. Injection pressure monitoring may provide a nonspecific warning of needle placement within or against a poorly compliant structure. However, preclinical evidence alone cannot establish whether it should be used routinely or whether it reduces nerve injury. No universal pressure threshold or clinically recommended injection rate can currently be defined.

papers.abstract: Propofol-based total intravenous anaesthesia (TIVA) is commonly used in neurovascular surgery, in which intraoperative neurophysiological monitoring limits inhalation anaesthetic use. However, propofol causes hypotension, and prolonged infusions can delay emergence. Remimazolam, a benzodiazepine whose effects are reversible with flumazenil, has been associated with less intraoperative hypotension than propofol, but its use raises concerns about postoperative delirium (POD). We tested whether remimazolam-based TIVA is noninferior to propofol-based TIVA for POD. In this single-centre, double-blind, randomised noninferiority trial, adults undergoing elective intracranial aneurysm clipping, arteriovenous malformation resection, microvascular decompression, or superficial temporal artery-middle cerebral artery bypass received remimazolam-based TIVA with flumazenil reversal at emergence, or propofol-based TIVA, both with remifentanil. The primary outcome was the cumulative incidence of POD within 5 days, assessed twice daily with the Confusion Assessment Method for the Intensive Care Unit (CAM-ICU) or the 3-Minute Diagnostic Interview for CAM-defined delirium (3D-CAM). The prespecified noninferiority margin was 10 percentage points. Among 686 patients in the modified intention-to-treat analysis, POD occurred in 44 of 344 (12.8%) with remimazolam and 37 of 342 (10.8%) with propofol (risk difference, 1.97 percentage points; 95% CI, -2.85 to 6.80; one-sided P<0.001 for noninferiority); per-protocol results were consistent. Hypotensive burden below a mean arterial pressure threshold of 65 mm Hg was lower in the remimazolam group (median, 0 vs 7.5 mm Hg min; P<0.001), and tracheal extubation in the operating room was more frequent (85.2% vs 67.3%). Remimazolam-based TIVA met the prespecified criterion for noninferiority to propofol-based TIVA with respect to postoperative delirium after elective neurovascular surgery. Interpretation should take into account that the observed incidence of postoperative delirium was lower than anticipated when the noninferiority margin was defined. NCT06115031 (ClinicalTrials.gov).

papers.abstract: Short-term peripheral nerve stimulation serves as a neuromodulation therapy that modulates neural activity to provide therapeutic benefit, particularly pain relief. This study investigated the effectiveness of short-term peripheral nerve stimulation as a minimally invasive approach for achieving pain relief. We systematically searched PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, Scopus, MEDLINE, Cochrane Library, and Google Scholar from database inception till September 10, 2026, for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) in adults comparing short-term peripheral nerve stimulation with sham stimulation or usual care. The primary outcome was the change in average pain intensity during the implantation period. Eight RCTs (543 participants) were included. Compared with the control group, the intervention group showed significant reductions in average pain intensity during the implantation period at 1-4 weeks (SMD = -0.48, 95% CI = -0.71 to -0.26, P < 0.0001) and 5-8 weeks (SMD = -0.96, 95% CI = -1.22 to -0.70, P < 0.0001), but no significant result after electrode removal. For worst pain intensity, the intervention group showed a greater reduction than the control group at all time periods except 1-4 weeks after EOT. Improvements in pain interference were delayed, becoming significant at 5-8 weeks during the implantation period (MD = -1.34, 95% CI = -1.86 to -0.82, P < 0.00001) and ≥8 weeks after the end of treatment (MD = -1.09, 95%CI = -1.69 to -0.50, P = 0.0003). Subgroup analyses showed improvements in postoperative pain. The usual care-controlled subgroup showed more pronounced and sustained benefits than the sham-controlled subgroup, and the chronic pain subgroup also showed more pronounced and sustained benefits compared to the acute/subacute pain subgroup. This meta-analysis provided preliminary evidence that short-term peripheral nerve stimulation may relieve pain during the implantation period, but not all outcomes suggest sustained improvements after electrode removal. papers.abstract: The Siglec-sialoglycan axis is an emerging glyco-immune checkpoint in cancer. This is supported by the frequent upregulation of both Siglecs and sialoglycans in the tumor microenvironment. Siglecs are receptors expressed on immune cells that recognize sialoglycans, carbohydrate structures terminated by sialic acid. Most Siglec receptor family members are inhibitory and suppress immune cell activation through the recruitment of SHP-1 and SHP-2 phosphatases. It is well established that Siglecs expressed by immune cells bind ligands present on other cells, including tumor and stromal cells (trans-interactions). However, immune cells themselves also express sialoglycans that can serve as ligands for Siglecs on the same cell surface (cis-interactions). Over the past two decades, numerous studies have addressed how Siglec trans-engagement facilitates immunosuppression in the tumor microenvironment. The role of cis-interactions in regulating Siglec function and their impact on immune cell activity, however, remains an underexplored topic for most Siglec family members. This review discusses how cis-ligands modulate Siglec function, the mechanisms regulating sialic acid expression on immune cell surfaces, and the functional relevance of cis-interactions expressed by immune cells in the tumor microenvironment. A better understanding of these processes may facilitate the development of next-generation therapeutics targeting the Siglec-sialoglycan axis in cancer.

papers.abstract: Importance Alterations in the fibroblast growth factor receptor (FGFR) pathway, particularly FGFR3 , are among the most common genomic events in urothelial carcinoma (UC) and represent a cornerstone of precision oncology. Although FGFR3 alterations predominate, selected FGFR2 fusions also identify patients who may benefit from targeted therapy. This review summarizes the biology, molecular diagnostics, and evolving clinical applications of FGFR alterations in UC. Observations FGFR2/3 alterations are clinically actionable biomarkers across non–muscle-invasive, muscle-invasive, metastatic, and upper-tract UC. Comprehensive genomic profiling, tissue sequencing, plasma circulating tumor DNA, urine-based molecular assays, and molecular residual disease assessment are expanding their roles in diagnosis, treatment selection, surveillance, and disease monitoring. Recent clinical studies support combination strategies, next-generation FGFR inhibitors, and earlier use of FGFR-directed therapy, while emerging technologies, including artificial intelligence–assisted pathology and integrated multi-omic biomarkers, may further improve patient selection. Conclusions and Relevance FGFR alterations have become integral to the molecular classification and precision management of UC. Continued advances in molecular diagnostics, liquid biopsy, biomarker-guided therapy, and next-generation FGFR inhibitors are expected to further personalize care. This review provides a practical framework for integrating FGFR biomarkers into contemporary management and highlights emerging developments likely to influence future clinical practice.

papers.abstract: Importance Primary bone cancers include multiple histologic types, with survival differing by age and location. Results from the Global Burden of Diseases, Injuries, and Risk Factors Study (GBD) 2023 were analyzed to support policies and initiatives worldwide. Objective To estimate the global burden of bone cancer from 1990 to 2023 and forecast future trends to 2050. Design, Setting, and Participants This systematic analysis estimated bone cancer incidence, mortality, and disability-adjusted life-years (DALYs) in 204 countries and territories grouped by GBD super-regions and World Bank income groups from 1990 to 2023, with forecasts through 2050. Individuals of all ages with bone cancers included in the GBD 2023 study were included in analyses. Data were analyzed from June 2023 to July 2025. Main Outcomes and Measures The GBD 2023 study used standardized estimation methods to describe bone cancer incidence, mortality, and DALYs in 2023, as well as trends over the past 3 decades and forecasts through 2050. All estimates are presented with 95% uncertainty intervals (UIs), and age-standardized rates (ASRs) were calculated using GBD-specific age weights. Results In 2023, there were 111 000 (95% UI, 81 300-164 000) malignant bone cancer cases, 76 600 (95% UI, 60 700-96 300) deaths, and 3.02 million (95% UI, 2.29 million-3.96 million) DALYs globally. A bimodal age distribution was noted in both incidence (peaking at ages 10 to 14 years and 65 to 69 years) and mortality (peaking at ages 15 to 19 years and 65 to 69 years). The highest ASRs for incidence were in Southeast Asia, East Asia, and Oceania (1.6 per 100 000; 95% UI, 1.1-2.4), while Sub-Saharan Africa had the highest ASRs for DALYs (51.0 per 100 000; 95% UI, 27.7-79.7). By World Bank income group, upper-middle–income countries had the highest ASRs for incidence, whereas low-income countries exhibited the highest ASRs for both mortality and DALYs. Globally, incident cases, deaths, and DALYs increased from 1990 to 2023, while global mortality and DALY ASRs were relatively stable; high-income countries experienced a decline in mortality and DALY ASRs. Forecasts suggest a potential increase in global cases and deaths by 2050. Conclusions and Relevance In this systematic analysis, the burden of bone cancer varied by age, geography, and time, underscoring global disparities. These findings provide valuable insights to inform health system planning and resource allocation tailored to different settings.

papers.abstract: Importance Consolidation immunotherapy improves outcomes after chemoradiotherapy for unresectable stage III non–small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). Disease progression remains common, and more effective consolidation strategies are needed. Objective To evaluate the efficacy and safety of benmelstobart with or without anlotinib as consolidation therapy after chemoradiotherapy for unresectable stage III NSCLC. Design, Setting, and Participants This multicenter double-blind phase 3 randomized clinical trial took place at 42 centers in China from 2020 to 2023 among patients with unresectable stage III NSCLC without progression after concurrent or sequential chemoradiotherapy. In stage 1, patients were randomized 1:1:1 to 2 active regimens or placebo; in stage 2, additional patients were randomized 1:1 between the active regimens to power their direct comparison. Data cutoffs were November 30, 2023, for stage 1 and July 8, 2024, for the pooled analysis. Data analysis was performed from January 17 to March 23, 2025. Interventions Patients were randomized to receive benmelstobart plus anlotinib, benmelstobart plus anlotinib placebo, or their matching placebos. Main Outcomes and Measures Primary end point was independent review committee (IRC)−assessed progression-free survival (PFS). Results Of 553 participants (median [IQR] age, 62 [56-67] years; 495 male individuals [89.5%]), 390 were randomized in stage 1 and 163 in stage 2. In stage 1, median PFS was 15.1 months (95% CI, 9.4-21.7) with benmelstobart plus anlotinib, 9.7 months (95% CI, 6.0-34.4) with benmelstobart alone, and 4.2 months (95% CI, 3.2-6.8) with placebo. The hazard ratios (HRs) were 0.49 (95% CI, 0.36-0.66; P &lt; .001) for benmelstobart plus anlotinib vs placebo and 0.53 (95% CI, 0.39-0.72; P &lt; .001) for benmelstobart vs placebo. In the pooled stage 1 and 2 analysis, median PFS was 17.4 (95% CI, 12.5-24.8) months with benmelstobart plus anlotinib and 11.2 (95% CI, 7.0-20.7) months with benmelstobart alone (HR, 0.82; 95% CI, 0.63-1.08; P = .12). Grade 3 to 5 treatment-related adverse events occurred in 48.8%, 29.4%, and 19.7% in the benmelstobart plus anlotinib, benmelstobart alone, and placebo groups, respectively; grade 5 events occurred in 7.2%, 1.4%, and 1.5%, respectively. Conclusions and Relevance This randomized clinical trial found that benmelstobart with or without anlotinib significantly improved PFS compared with placebo. Adding anlotinib did not significantly improve PFS compared with benmelstobart alone and increased severe and fatal treatment-related adverse events. papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Introduction Pulmonary carcinoids (PCs) are rare, well‐differentiated, neuroendocrine lung tumors with limited treatment options for advanced disease, underscoring the need for targeted therapies. PCs typically exhibit a low mutational burden. Although MEN1 and chromatin‐modifier mutations are known contributors, potentially actionable alterations remain poorly characterized. To better define therapeutic opportunities, we evaluated oncogenic fusions and variants across 17 cancer‐associated genes in a large retrospective PC cohort. Methods Formalin‐fixed, paraffin‐embedded primary tumors from Helsinki University Hospital ( n = 119, collected between 1990 and 2020) were subjected to targeted RNA‐based fusion and variant analysis using the Archer FusionPlex Lung v2 assay. Results The most frequent recurrent genetic rearrangements involved ALK ( n = 5), BRAF ( n = 3), FGFR2 ( n = 3), and NTRK3 ( n = 2), each featuring diverse fusion partners. Variant analysis identified BRAF , EGFR , FGFR1 , and FGFR3 as the most frequently mutated genes, although only 2.2% ( n = 4) of all detected variants were classified as oncogenic. Notably, 66.7% of all oncogenic or likely oncogenic variants occurred in BRAF and EGFR . Oncogenic variants were identified in ALK , BRAF , EGFR , and ERBB2 . Although all FGFR1–3 variants were of uncertain significance, their frequency (34.1% of all detected variants), together with the three FGFR2 fusions, suggested that FGFR alterations may be biologically relevant in PCs. Conclusion Despite the typically muted genomic landscape of PCs, our study revealed a small yet therapeutically relevant subset of alterations. The findings further characterized the molecular profile of PCs and identified potentially actionable molecular subgroups. While these alterations were not associated with disease‐specific survival or metastatic status, they support consideration of molecular profiling in selected patients with advanced disease.

papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Background The partial volume effect influences the results of volumetrics performed on MRI sequences with different slice thicknesses. Although a standardized brain tumor imaging protocol with high‐quality 1 mm slices is recommended, segmentation is still commonly performed on thicker slices, especially in retrospective studies. We aimed to quantify the impact of different slice thicknesses on volumetric measurements of brain tumors, using treatment‐naive glioblastoma as a representative example. Methods Volumes were measured on T1‐weighted contrast‐enhanced (CE) sequences using semiautomatic segmentation across three predefined slice thicknesses: 1 mm (“thin”; reference measurement), 3 mm (“intermediate”), and 5 mm (“thick”). Data from 46 patients with the availability of all three slice thicknesses were statistically analyzed, including repeated‐measures ANOVA with post hoc comparisons, Bland–Altman analysis, correlations, and linear regression. Results The tumor volumes measured increased with slice thickness, with mean values of 36.4 cm 3 (“thin”), 38.6 cm 3 (“intermediate”), and 41.0 cm 3 (“thick”). Repeated measures ANOVA showed significant differences between groups ( p < 0.01). The mean deviation of the tumor volumes on “thick” relative to “thin” slices was 16% (±10%). Bland–Altman analysis and linear regression confirmed systematically higher measured volumes on “thick” slices. Tumor size on “thin” slices correlated negatively with the percentage deviation on “thick” slices ( r = −0.56; p < 0.01). Conclusion Volumetric measurements obtained from “thick” slices showed systematically higher tumor volumes and greater variability relative to the 1 mm reference. Volumetric data obtained from different slice thicknesses should not be combined, or concepts for adjustment should be considered to maintain methodological consistency and reliability in volumetric studies. We advocate the use of high‐quality 3D 1 mm imaging for volumetric analysis whenever possible.

papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Background Prostate‐specific antigen (PSA) and PSA density (PSAD) are widely used for prostate cancer (PCa) screening, but their diagnostic thresholds have not been differentially adjusted for ethnic groups in clinical practice. This multicenter study aimed to establish the distribution of PSA and PSAD in Chinese men without PCa and compare these values with published data from African American (AA) and Caucasian American (CA) men to assess potential racial disparities. Methods We analyzed 528 biopsy‐negative Chinese men from two tertiary centers, comparing their age‐adjusted PSA/PSAD with published AA/CA data. Additionally, we compared PSA/PSAD distributions and the proportion of men exceeding the conventional PSA cutoff (4 ng/mL) across racial groups. Results PSA levels showed a weak but significant positive correlation with age ( r = 0.121, p = 0.005), whereas PSAD did not ( r = −0.032, p = 0.465). Notably, Chinese men without PCa exhibited significantly higher mean PSA and PSAD than AA and CA men (PSA: 17.28 vs. 7.97 vs. 4.30 ng/mL, p < 0.001; PSAD: 0.28 vs. 0.19 vs. 0.11 ng/mL/mL, p < 0.001). Using a PSA cutoff of 4 ng/mL, the specificity for PCa detection was substantially lower in Chinese men than in AA and CA men at matched sensitivity levels. Conclusions This study reveals striking racial differences in baseline PSA and PSAD among men without PCa, with Chinese men demonstrating markedly higher values than AA and CA counterparts. These findings challenge the universal application of current PSA thresholds and underscore the need for race‐specific adjustments to optimize PCa screening accuracy.

papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Alterations in the composition of the gut microbiota have been associated with colorectal cancer (CRC), with growing evidence indicating that specific microbes can have an impact on the tumour microenvironment. In this study, we investigated the associations of an oral pathobiont consortium comprising P. stomatis , F. nucleatum sensu lato and P. micra with the tumour immune microenvironment and the clinical presentation of CRC patients. Bacterial levels were quantified in fresh frozen tumour tissues using qPCR and the tumour immune environment was analysed using multiplex immunohistochemistry and multispectral imaging, profiling cytotoxic T cells, T‐helper 1 cells, regulatory T cells, B cells, macrophages and regulatory immune checkpoint molecules (CTLA‐4, PD‐1 and PD‐L1). Tumours with polymicrobial intratumoural co‐occurrence were more frequently right‐sided and exhibited microsatellite instability compared with tumours containing low bacterial levels or high levels of F. nucleatum sensu lato alone. Furthermore, polymicrobial tumours exhibited an altered tumour immune microenvironment, with decreased infiltration of FOXP3 + T regulatory cells and CD68 + macrophages, and increased tumour cell expression of PD‐L1 in the tumour centre. Polymicrobial tumours were also associated with poorer patient survival. In conclusion, our findings suggest a link between the co‐occurrence of P. stomatis , F. nucleatum sensu lato and P. micra and an altered tumour immune microenvironment in CRC. Elucidating the relationship between bacterial species and immune marker expression may enable the development of improved prognostic and predictive biomarkers, as well as new possibilities for therapeutic intervention.

papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Background Component C1q binding protein (C1QBP) is known as an important regulator of mitochondrial plasticity and is involved in antitumor immune response in cancers. Nevertheless, its role in lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) still remains largely unknown. Methods C1QBP expression in LUAD and adjacent normal samples was compared by Wilcoxon test, and the corresponding receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve was used to estimate its diagnostic value. Associations between C1QBP expression levels and different clinical traits were analyzed by chi‐square test; K‐M curves were applied for analyzing survival differences, and univariate and multivariate Cox analysis were employed to construct the C1QBP ‐related nomogram model. Furthermore, GSEA and immune analysis were performed to explore the mechanism. Finally, rhC1QBP was applied to cultured mast cells in vivo to investigate its regulatory effect on mast cell dysfunction, and sh‐C1QBP was injected into LUAD xenograft mice to explore the effect of C1QBP knockdown on tumor growth in vivo. Results The C1QBP expression level, with a preferable diagnosis effect, was significantly different between LUAD and normal samples, and was notably interrelated with gender, TNM stage, and Fustat in LUAD patients. LUAD patients with high C1QBP levels displayed lower survival rates. Our nomogram based on C1QBP expression and T stage displayed decent prediction capability. There was a significant difference in C1QBP expression in plasma cells, regulatory T cells (Tregs), activated CD4 memory T cells, resting mast cells, and eosinophils between LUAD patients and the controls. Upregulation of C1QBP with rhC1QBP treatment promoted mast cell ferroptosis through interacting with the Cullin3 protein. While Fer‐1, a ferroptosis inhibitor, counteracted rhC1QBP induced ferroptosis in mast cells. Knockdown of C1QBP inhibited tumor growth in xenograft mice. Conclusion C1QBP may be a promising potential prognostic biomarker in LUAD and a potential therapeutic target by affecting the immune microenvironment of LUAD patients.

papers.abstract: Gastroesophageal junction cancer is a rising global health concern with variable outcomes. The availability to high-volume cancer centers may influence survival, yet disparities related to geography and socioeconomic status remain poorly defined. A retrospective cohort study was conducted using the SEER 21 Research Plus database (2000-2022). A total of 40,273 patients with locoregional gastroesophageal junction cancer were included. Patient-level variables included age, sex, race, histology, stage, and survival. Socioeconomic and geographic variables included county-level median household income and rural-urban residence. State-level volume was defined according to the number of high-volume esophageal cancer centers within each patient's state of residence: high-volume (≥ 2 centers), moderate-volume (1 center), and low-volume (no centers). The primary outcome was overall survival. Cox proportional hazards models were used to evaluate associations between patient-, socioeconomic-, geographic-, and state-level factors and survival. Residence in states with lower-volume centers was associated with worse outcomes than residence in states with high-volume centers. Each step toward lower-volume categories was associated with an increased hazard of death (HR 0.923, 95% CI 0.899-0.949, p < 0.001). While stage at diagnosis varied significantly across hospital volume categories (p < 0.001), no clear pattern of more advanced stage in lower-volume states was observed. Patients with adenocarcinoma had a 25% lower hazard of death compared to those with squamous cell carcinoma (HR 0.752, 95% CI 0.726-0.780, p < 0.001). Female gender was associated with a statistically significant increase in hazard of death compared to males (HR 1.042, 95% CI 1.013-1.072, p = 0.004). Additionally, higher median household income was associated with improved survival (HR 1.006, p < 0.001 per category increase), and urban residence (HR 1.036, p < 0.001) was independently associated with improved survival. Survival in locoregional gastroesophageal junction cancer is influenced by both tumor biology and healthcare access. Residence in states with high-volume centers, adenocarcinoma histology, higher income, and urban residence were independently associated with improved survival, highlighting disparities tied to regional resource availability within the United States.

papers.abstract: Colon and rectal neuroendocrine tumors (NETs) have varying disease behaviors, presentations, and outcomes. Rectal NETs are detected early; colonic NETs present later and more aggressively. We compared demographic, tumor, treatment, and survival characteristics of colonic versus rectal NETs. This retrospective cohort study used SEER data (2000-2022) to identify adults with colonic or rectal NETs. Demographic, tumor, and treatment characteristics were compared by tumor site. Five-year overall survival (OS) and cancer-specific survival (CSS) were analyzed using Kaplan-Meier statistics and multivariable Cox proportional hazards regression. Additional site-specific analyses evaluated stage and treatment patterns by race, ethnicity, and household income. Twenty-four percent of 30 246 patients had colonic NETs, and 76.0% had rectal NETs. Rectal NET patients were younger (55.7 vs. 62.9 years, p < 0.001) and more often Black, Asian, or Hispanic. Colonic NETs were more frequently poorly differentiated (43.9% vs. 7.0%), larger (median 30 vs. 5 mm), and more likely to have liver metastases (27.7% vs. 3.7%). Rectal NETs underwent local excision (92.1%), colonic NETs required colectomy (72.3%). Rectal NETs demonstrated higher 5-year OS (88.8% vs. 55.8%) and CSS (93.8% vs. 58.2%, p < 0.001). Stage III colonic NETs had higher CSS than rectal NETs (67.3% vs. 53.5%, p < 0.001). Colonic and rectal NETs have distinct clinicopathologic profiles, treatment patterns, and stage-specific outcomes. These findings support site-specific evaluation while emphasizing the importance of stage and tumor biology in prognosis.

papers.abstract: Core needle biopsy (CNB) is commonly used to diagnose bone tumors, but characteristics of tibial lesions may affect its diagnostic performance. We evaluated the diagnostic performance of CT-guided CNB for tibial lesions, factors associated with diagnostic success, and outcomes of nondiagnostic biopsies. We retrospectively reviewed 272 patients with tibial lesions treated at a quaternary sarcoma referral center from 2016 to 2022, of whom 43 underwent CT-guided CNB. Patient, lesion, and pathologic characteristics were evaluated for associations with diagnostic outcomes. Of 43 biopsies, 58.1% were diagnostic, 79.1% accurate, and 55.8% successful. Accuracy was significantly higher for non-diaphyseal than diaphyseal lesions (27/31 vs. 7/12; p = 0.038). Lesions < 5 cm were less likely to achieve diagnostic success than lesions ≥ 5 cm (OR 0.231, 95% CI 0.064-0.836; p = 0.022). Of 18 nondiagnostic CNBs, 12 underwent subsequent incisional biopsy, identifying five malignancies. CT-guided CNB of tibial lesions has modest diagnostic yield, with lower accuracy in diaphyseal lesions and reduced diagnostic success in lesions < 5 cm. These findings may inform biopsy planning and identify patients more likely to require incisional biopsy for definitive diagnosis.

papers.abstract: To evaluate the incidence, timing and anatomical pattern of relapse after cytoreductive surgery (CRS) for pseudomyxoma peritonei (PMP), and identify predictors of overall and early (within 12 months) relapse. Retrospective cohort study of consecutive patients undergoing curative-intent CRS for appendiceal PMP at a single institution (2016-2025), recording the site of first relapse. Predictors of progression-free survival (PFS) and early relapse were evaluated using Cox and logistic regression. Among 204 patients, CC-0/1 cytoreduction was achieved in 89% and HIPEC in 92%. At 37.1-month median follow-up, 89 patients (44%) relapsed; 3-year PFS and overall survival were 50.2% and 75.6%. Relapse was predominantly intraperitoneal, most often the pelvis and small bowel/mesentery (25% each). Histology and completeness of cytoreduction independently predicted PFS: low-grade (HR 2.18), high-grade (HR 2.79) and signet-ring PMP (HR 4.35) vs acellular mucin, CC-2/3 (HR 2.18), and male sex (HR 1.74). Early relapse occurred in 34 patients (17%), independently predicted by high-grade histology (OR 5.06) and CC-2/3 (OR 3.55). Relapse after CRS for PMP is predominantly intraperitoneal, most often the small bowel/mesentery and pelvis. Histology and completeness of cytoreduction are the principal determinants of overall and early relapse, supporting risk-stratified surveillance and selective repeat cytoreduction.

papers.abstract: Colorectal cancer (CRC) metastases to retroperitoneal (RP) and lateral pelvic (LP) lymph nodes are functionally classified as stage IV disease. While metastasectomy is established for select hepatic and pulmonary metastases, the role of lymphadenectomy for nodal disease remains uncertain. This study evaluates the safety, indications, and oncologic outcomes of RP/LP lymph node dissection in CRC. A single-center retrospective review identified patients undergoing RP or LP lymphadenectomy for CRC between 2011 and 2024. Patients with peritoneal metastases or incomplete data were excluded. Demographic, operative, and outcome data were analyzed. Associations with nodal positivity, recurrence-free survival (RFS), and overall survival (OS) were assessed using Fisher's exact test and univariate Cox regression. Forty-nine patients underwent lymphadenectomy, 45% for synchronous and 55% for metachronous nodal metastases. Dissection was selective in 61% and formal in 39%, with 86% undergoing concurrent major abdominal procedures. There was no perioperative mortality and dissection-specific morbidity was low (two lymphatic leaks, both after multivisceral resection). Pathologic nodal metastases were confirmed in 59% of cases. Median RFS and OS were 30.2 and 104.9 months, respectively. Node positivity was associated with initial N2 stage but did not affect RFS or OS. Formal lymphadenectomy was associated with shorter RFS, likely reflecting higher disease burden. RP and LP lymphadenectomy can be safely performed, even with multivisceral resection. Pathologic nodal status did not predict survival, suggesting potential benefit to lymphadenectomy irrespective of final pathology. These findings support its use in carefully selected patients with controlled systemic disease and isolated nodal recurrence.

papers.abstract: With ongoing axillary treatment de-escalation in breast cancer, preoperative assessment of axillary tumor burden has become increasingly important. We investigated whether pathological information from preoperative axillary lymph node (LN) core needle biopsy (CNB) could stratify final axillary tumor burden. We included 473 patients who underwent ultrasound-guided CNB of suspicious axillary LNs. Associations of metastatic focus size and extranodal extension (ENE) on CNB with final axillary tumor burden were evaluated. Of 473 patients, 212 had positive and 261 had negative CNB findings. Among 135 CNB-positive patients undergoing upfront surgery, CNB metastatic focus size correlated with the maximum metastatic focus size in resected LNs (ρ = 0.72, p < 0.001) and the number of positive LNs (ρ = 0.269, p = 0.0016). All 21 patients with a CNB metastatic focus ≤ 2 mm had two or fewer positive LNs. ENE independently predicted pN2-3 disease (OR, 3.61; 95% CI, 1.51-8.68; p = 0.004). Among patients receiving primary systemic therapy, CNB metastatic focus size did not independently predict total pathological complete response. None of 244 CNB-negative patients undergoing upfront surgery had pN2 or higher disease. Pathological information from preoperative axillary LN CNB may help stratify axillary tumor burden and support individualized axillary risk assessment in the era of treatment de-escalation.

papers.abstract: Transoral robotic thyroidectomy (TORT) is a promising alternative to open thyroidectomy (OT) for managing differentiated thyroid carcinoma (DTC), especially in select low-risk patients. This study aimed to compare TORT and OT in patients with DTC < 2 cm using propensity score matching. A retrospective analysis of 355 patients who underwent thyroidectomy between April 2020 and August 2024 was conducted. Of these, 100 underwent TORT and 255 underwent OT. Propensity score matching (1:1) yielded 70 patients per group. Outcomes included operative time, lymph node retrieval, complications, and hospital stay. TORT had significantly longer operative times than OT (151.2 ± 42.1 vs. 48.3 ± 11.1 min; p 0.05). Hospital stay was slightly longer for TORT (2.1 ± 0.7 vs. 1.8 ± 0.7 days; p = 0.011). No recurrences were observed during the median follow-up period of 29 months in the TORT group and 44 months in the OT group (p = 0.238). TORT demonstrated comparable short-term oncologic and surgical outcomes to OT in well-selected patients with DTC < 2 cm. Further studies with longer follow-up are needed to confirm long-term oncologic safety.

papers.abstract: Chemo-, radio-, and targeted therapies can induce a stable growth arrest known as therapy-induced senescence (TIS), which may be therapeutically exploited using senolytic compounds that selectively eliminate senescent cells. Children with BRAF-V600E-driven brain tumours are commonly treated with low-dose chemotherapies and MAPK inhibitors, alone or in combination, often with good initial responses. However, a majority of patients experiences tumour regrowth following treatment withdrawal. Here, we investigate the contribution of TIS to treatment response and relapse, and assess the therapeutic potential of senolytics in preclinical models of paediatric BRAF-V600E glioma. Preclinical models of paediatric low-grade glioma were analysed in vitro or following orthotopic transplantation into mice and treated with Dabrafenib, Trametinib, Tovorafenib or Vinblastine. Senescence was assessed using molecular and cytological markers. Sensitivity to senolytic compounds was evaluated using in vitro dose-response assays and in vivo treatment studies. Trametinib induced a robust senescent phenotype in BT-40 tumours in vivo, characterised by activation of a senescence-associated secretory phenotype and expansion of IBA-1-positive myeloid cells. In vitro, senescence was induced in BT-40 cells following treatment with MAPK inhibitors and Vinblastine, and was similarly observed in H9-derived human neural stem cells expressing BRAF-V600E. Navitoclax was identified as a potent senolytic against senescent BT-40 cells, primarily through inhibition of the anti-apoptotic protein BCL-xL. In vivo, combined Trametinib and Navitoclax treatment ablated senescent tumour cells, significantly reduced tumour regrowth after treatment withdrawal, and improved survival. These findings demonstrate that Navitoclax enhances Trametinib's anti-tumour efficacy and limits tumour relapse following treatment cessation.

papers.abstract: Abstract Background U.S. Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) lung cancer screening (LCS) eligibility relies on smoking history data that are often incomplete or inaccurate in Electronic Health Records (EHRs). Inaccurate data combined with clinicians’ unfamiliarity with LCS recommendations may lead to guideline-discordant screening, potentially reducing the benefit-risk ratio and misallocating resources. Limited data exist that describe USPSTF-ineligible patients who receive and complete LCS orders. Methods We conducted a retrospective cohort study of adults receiving an LCS order at Kaiser Permanente Colorado (5/1/2014-12/31/2023). Using structured EHR data to determine eligibility, we assessed USPSTF-ineligible LCS orders, screening completion rates, and lung cancer yield. Results Of 15,624 patients receiving LCS orders, 2,048 (13%) were classified as USPSTF-ineligible. Most ineligibility resulted from incomplete (28%) or out-of-range smoking history data (54%). USPSTF-ineligible patients were more likely to be female and affluent and less likely to be White, aged 55-80, or currently smoke. Orders were more common during program rollout and the COVID-19 pandemic. Among ineligible patients, 47% completed screening; 3% were diagnosed with lung cancer, 67% at an early stage. Lung cancer detection was 8% among Positive screens (Lung-RADS 3-4) and 1% among Negative screens (Lung-RADS 1-2). Conclusions A substantial proportion of patients receiving lung cancer screening orders were classified as USPSTF-ineligible using structured EHR data, primarily because of incomplete or out-of-range smoking histories. The unexpectedly high lung cancer detection rate suggests that many may have been misclassified rather than truly ineligible. These findings highlight the challenges of utilizing EHR data to identify guideline-discordant screening rates.

papers.abstract: Patients receiving maintenance hemodialysis (HD) have limited physiologic reserve and high competing cardiometabolic risk, yet surgery remains central to cure for many gastrointestinal (GI) malignancies. Evidence describing oncologic surgery in this population is fragmented across cancer sites and data sources. A PRISMA guided systematic review of adult patients on maintenance HD undergoing resection for GI malignancy was performed. The review searched PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and CENTRAL through March 2026 and included comparative observational studies reporting perioperative or long-term outcomes. In parallel, a propensity-score matched TriNetX cohort of adults undergoing major GI cancer surgery between 2010 and 2025. HD was defined by preoperative ESRD and dialysis dependence codes. Patients were matched 1:1 on age, sex, race, and ethnicity. The primary outcome was 30-day mortality; secondary outcomes were 30-day sepsis, pneumonia, and acute myocardial infarction (AMI). The review included 20 studies after screening 1,744 deduplicated records and 83 full texts. Colorectal surgery provided the most robust evidence: dialysis was associated with markedly higher mortality and serious morbidity, and a published meta-analysis of colorectal surgery estimated a pooled mortality odds ratio (OR) of 4.12. Gastric, pancreatic, and hepatobiliary reports were smaller but showed the same direction of effect, with frequent infectious and cardiovascular complications and substantial competing non-cancer mortality. In the current TriNetX analysis, 3,757 HD patients were matched to 3757 non-HD controls. Thirty-day mortality was 11.4% in HD patients versus 3.0% in controls (OR: 4.21, 95% CI: 3.40-5.22). HD patients also had higher rates of sepsis (14.1% vs. 3.9%; OR 4.06), pneumonia (8.1% vs. 2.2%; OR: 4.02), and AMI (4.3% vs. 0.9%; OR: 5.18). Across GI cancer operations, maintenance HD identifies a very high-risk surgical phenotype. The dominant short-term pattern is excess death, infection, and cardiopulmonary morbidity; the dominant long-term pattern is competing non-cancer mortality. Surgery remains appropriate for selected patients with resectable disease, but perioperative dialysis timing, multidisciplinary optimization, and treatment in experienced centers are critical.

papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Neoadjuvant therapy has become an integral component of the multidisciplinary management of resectable non–small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). The introduction of immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) has transformed the perioperative treatment landscape by improving pathological response rates, reducing the risk of recurrence, and offering the potential for durable survival benefits. In recent years, multiple neoadjuvant strategies, including ICI monotherapy, chemoimmunotherapy, dual immune checkpoint blockade, and combinations with radiotherapy, anti‐angiogenic agents, or targeted therapies, have been actively investigated to further optimize treatment efficacy. Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) are reshaping neoadjuvant strategies for resectable NSCLC. LCMC3 confirmed the feasibility of ICIs monotherapy, while CheckMate 816 and NADIM demonstrated that ICI–chemotherapy combinations markedly improve major pathological response and survival outcomes. Emerging perioperative studies, including CheckMate 77 T and AEGEAN, further support the integration of immunotherapy into standard treatment paradigms. Radiotherapy enhances tumor immunogenicity and shows synergy with ICIs, as highlighted in PACIFIC and KEYNOTE‐799. Although clinical evidence for ICI–anti‐angiogenic combinations remains preliminary, their mechanistic rationale is strong. In EGFR‐ or ALK‐altered NSCLC, emerging data suggest that neoadjuvant targeted therapy and carefully selected immunotherapy‐based strategies may further improve disease control while delaying recurrence. Despite these advances, several challenges remain, including the paucity of long‐term survival data, discordance between pathological responses and clinical benefit, treatment‐related toxicities, optimal treatment sequencing, biomarker‐guided patient selection, and mechanisms of primary or acquired resistance. Advances in predictive modeling based on PD‐L1 expression, tumor mutational burden (TMB), radiomics, nomograms, circulating tumor DNA, and multi‐omics biomarkers, together with a deeper understanding of metabolic–immune crosstalk, are expected to facilitate precision perioperative immunotherapy. This review comprehensively summarizes current evidence regarding neoadjuvant immunotherapy strategies for resectable NSCLC, highlights pivotal clinical trial findings, discusses emerging combination approaches and predictive biomarkers, and outlines future research directions aimed at improving personalized treatment and long‐term patient outcomes.

papers.abstract: Radiotherapy can enhance anti-tumor immunity by modulating the tumor microenvironment. However, its direct effects on dendritic cells (DCs) as key antigen-presenting cells remain poorly studied. Although DCs are considered relatively radioresistant, their functional capacity following irradiation is controversial and likely subset-dependent. In this study, we systematically analyzed the radiosensitivity and post-irradiation functional capacity of murine bone marrow-derived conventional type 1 DCs (cDC1s), which play a pivotal role in initiating CD8+ T cell-mediated anti-tumor immunity, conventional type 2 DCs (cDC2s), and monocyte-derived DCs (MoDCs) in vitro. After irradiation, DC viability and surface marker expression were assessed. To evaluate functional competence, DCs were stimulated with high hydrostatic pressure-inactivated tumor cells in combination with the adjuvants poly I:C and α-CD40 as a model system for therapeutic tumor vaccination, and the phagocytic activity, activation, and cytokine/chemokine secretion of the DCs were analyzed. DC radiosensitivity depended strongly on both the subset and maturation state, with mature DCs showing higher radioresistance than their immature counterparts, and with immature cDC1s being particularly more susceptible. Nevertheless, surviving DCs retained their ability to phagocytose tumor cells and, upon stimulation, upregulate activation- and migration-associated markers and secrete cytokines and chemokines. In vivo, radio-immunotherapy promoted DC migration to the tumor-draining lymph node and induced DC activation, as indicated by elevated concentrations of DC-related cytokines in the peripheral blood. Within a fixed radiotherapy plus checkpoint inhibition regimen, tumor growth delay was largely preserved in Batf3-/- mice, lacking the cDC1 subset. Collectively, irradiation does not abrogate DC function, and anti-tumor immunity in radio-immunotherapy does not strictly require cDC1s.

papers.abstract: Multidisciplinary management of locally advanced rectal cancer (LARC) has evolved rapidly over the past decade, guided by data from multiple prospective clinical trials. Changes in treatment of cT3-4 or N+ rectal cancer at a comprehensive cancer center between 2015 and 2023 were analyzed retrospectively. Of 1121 patients who received neoadjuvant therapy, 793 (71%) underwent active surveillance and 328 (29%) underwent surgery within 3 months. Treatments whose use increased from 2015 to 2023 included TNT with consolidation chemotherapy (from 10% to 81%), neoadjuvant chemotherapy alone (from 13% to 21%), immunotherapy or targeted therapy (from 0% to 10%), and oral capecitabine versus intravenous fluorouracil in combination with oxaliplatin (from 4% to 56%). Among patients who received TNT, nonoperative management with sustained clinical complete response rose from 38% to 50%. With more patients undergoing nonoperative management, the rate of pathologic complete response decreased from 22% to 8.3%. Robotic assistance was used in 88% of surgeries. The adoption of new diagnostic and treatment paradigms allows for longer intervals until surgery, more frequent use of active surveillance, and higher rates of organ preservation without compromising safety or oncologic outcomes.

papers.abstract: Abstract Vasculogenic mimicry (VM) is a process in which malignant cells acquire endothelial-like functions to generate perfusable vascular channels independent of endothelial cells. VM represents a major barrier to effective vascular endothelial growth factor A (VEGFA)-targeted therapy in cancer. In this study, we used organ-scale vascular imaging that identified a mechanism of VM in glioblastoma (GBM) mediated by alpha-L-fucosidase 1 (FUCA1). FUCA1 was preferentially expressed in glioblastoma stem-like cells (GSCs) with high CD44 expression. FUCA1 functioned as a key regulator of GSC-mediated VM by stabilizing LDHA protein and promoting a metabolic shift toward glycolysis. Elevated glycolytic flux increased lactate production and enhanced histone H3 lysine 18 lactylation (H3K18la), which in turn activated SERPINF1 transcription and drove VM in GSCs. In preclinical models, the FUCA1 inhibitor deoxyfuconojirimycin hydrochloride (DFH) significantly reduced GSC tumorigenicity and VM in vivo and exhibited robust antitumor activity when combined with anti-VEGFA therapy. Collectively, these findings define a FUCA1-mediated histone lactylation pathway that enhances GSC VM and highlight a therapeutically targetable mechanism to improve the efficacy of current anti-angiogenic strategies in GBM.

papers.abstract: Abstract KRAS inhibitors (KRASi) are reshaping the treatment of aggressive tumors such as pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC), but it is appreciated that patients will eventually acquire resistance through multiple pathways. To avoid this outcome, there is much effort to identify combination therapies that take advantage of the ‘window-of-opportunity’ permitted from KRAS inhibition. Tumor cell-intrinsic targeting – as a result of KRASi – results in altered immune and stromal features within the PDAC tumor site that could allow for improved, non-KRAS-targeted, treatment efficacy. Qiang and colleagues investigate the potential of pairing KRASi with immunotherapy – here, an IL-21 mimic – for therapeutic benefit during this ‘open window’ phase of the KRASi-induced tumor debulking. IL-21 promotes a CD4 T cell response that requires both conventional type 2 dendritic cells (cDC2s) and interferon (IFN)-γ, but not direct tumor cell recognition via major histocompatibility complex (MHC). This work fits in a series of studies highlighting the ability to drive PDAC tumor rejection through cytokines derived from CD4, but not CD8, T cells. These findings highlight a divergence from more ‘traditional’ immunotherapeutic responses, where cytotoxic CD8 T cells have historically dominated tumor control. Identifying alternative paths towards targeting PDAC may be beneficial – and points towards cell types and modalities that could be leveraged for clinical benefit as the field identifies potential combinatorial partners for KRASi and more patients start receiving these drugs.

papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Background Non‐pharmacological interventions are essential to reduce procedural anxiety in pediatric care. Fidget and sensory toys are widely used for distraction and self‐regulation, yet evidence on their effectiveness remains fragmented. This scoping review mapped the evidence on fidget and sensory toys across general pediatric settings, with a focus on perioperative outcomes—such as anxiety, distress, and pain—to highlight relevant gaps in care. Methods This scoping review followed the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) methodology and the PRISMA‐ScR guidelines. Searches were conducted in MEDLINE/PubMed, EMBASE, Scopus, Web of Science, and Cochrane CENTRAL, complemented by trial registries, gray literature, citation tracking, and reference screening. Studies involving children (0–18 years) evaluating fidget or sensory toys in any setting were eligible. Two independent reviewers performed study selection and data extraction. Findings Fifteen studies published between 2017 and 2026 met the inclusion criteria. Fidget spinners were the most frequently investigated device ( n = 9), followed by stress balls ( n = 3). Studies were conducted in educational ( n = 8) and healthcare settings ( n = 7). Educational studies generally reported limited or no benefits for attention, engagement, behavior, or academic performance. In contrast, healthcare studies generally suggested reductions in anxiety, pain, fear, and procedural distress, although findings were heterogeneous, and outcome measures varied substantially. Conclusions Current evidence does not support the routine use of fidget toys to improve attention or academic performance in educational settings. Evidence from healthcare and procedural settings suggests that fidget and sensory toys may be feasible distraction tools for selected pediatric patients, but evidence is insufficient to support routine perioperative use. Further high‐quality randomized controlled trials are needed to establish standardized intervention protocols and identify the pediatric populations and clinical settings most likely to benefit.

papers.abstract: Synaptic transmission impairment and neuronal loss are hallmarks of neurodegenerative diseases (NDDs). To date, the absence of effective therapies for treating or preventing NDDs underscores the critical need to comprehend the mechanisms underlying synaptic loss and impairment to develop novel interventions. Synaptic transmission is a complex communication process between presynaptic and postsynaptic neurons. Separate postsynaptic receptors activated by a variety of neurotransmitters initiate different downstream signaling cascades that are modulated by receptor-associated auxiliary subunits. Moreover, glia-neuron interactions and various neuropeptides can also modulate diverse synaptic functions. In this review, we first summarize the presynaptic and postsynaptic regulatory mechanisms of synaptic transmission in glutamatergic, GABAergic, cholinergic, and dopaminergic neurons in NDDs. We then emphasize the fundamental role of microglia and astrocytes in maintaining neuronal homeostasis and discuss how glia-neuron cross-talk affects synaptic and neuronal function throughout the pathological processes of NDDs, as well as how aging accelerates synaptic dysfunction in NDDs. We also highlight therapeutic strategies aimed at preserving or restoring synaptic integrity, including approaches that enhance plasticity, fine‑tune neurotransmitter signaling, or target immune pathways. Finally, we evaluate the current state of research for each intervention class and consider the major obstacles and opportunities that lie ahead in developing effective synapse‑directed therapies for NDDs.

papers.abstract: Small cell lung cancer (SCLC) remains one of the most lethal thoracic malignancies, characterized by rapid progression, early metastasis, and limited durable responses to conventional therapy. Delta-like ligand 3 (DLL3), a Notch pathway inhibitory ligand aberrantly overexpressed on the surface of approximately 70-85% of SCLC tumor cells but largely absent from normal adult tissue, has emerged as a compelling and therapeutically actionable target. Early efforts to exploit DLL3 through the antibody-drug conjugate (ADC) rovalpituzumab tesirine (Rova-T) yielded important mechanistic insights despite failing to demonstrate survival benefit in phase III trials and have since catalyzed a new generation of more refined DLL3-directed strategies. This review critically examines the evolving portfolio of DLL3-targeted therapies across three principal modalities: T-cell engagers, ADCs, and chimeric antigen receptor T-cell (CAR-T) therapies. In parallel, we examine emerging non-DLL3 therapeutic strategies reshaping the broader SCLC landscape. We additionally discuss the translational science underpinning DLL3 as a biomarker, including the emerging roles of circulating tumor cell-based liquid biopsy and DLL3-directed immunoPET-CT imaging in patient selection and treatment monitoring.

papers.abstract: Diabetic kidney disease (DKD) is the leading cause of end-stage kidney disease worldwide. However, albuminuria and estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), which define and stage DKD, report established injury and do not resolve the cellular heterogeneity underlying variable progression. Urine, the only biofluid to traverse every nephron segment, carries shed cells, extracellular vesicles (EVs) and cell-free DNA (cfDNA), each retaining information about its cell of origin. This review develops the concept of a digital urinary biopsy, in which the three compartments are read together against spatial single-cell kidney atlases to infer non-invasively which cell states are active and whether niche-associated programs are engaged, an approach we term atlas-anchored molecular profiling. For each compartment, we tabulate study population, sample size, processing, assay, performance and validation status. Because shed-cell RNA, selectively sorted vesicle cargo and cfDNA methylation differ in origin, measurement scale and bias, each requires its own reference matrix, sampling function and background terms. All three carry renal information in feasibility studies, yet none is a validated clinical assay in DKD. Moreover, a cfDNA methylation reference at the required resolution is lacking, and no named computational method has been tested on urine. We therefore present the framework as a structured research hypothesis and define the required validation, from analytical and clinical validity to prospective demonstration of utility, with non-albuminuric DKD, which albuminuria-based screening misses, as the index use case. It offers a testable route to cell-resolved, non-invasive staging of DKD rather than a demonstrated capability.

papers.abstract: Abstract Enhancer of zeste homolog 2 (EZH2), the catalytic subunit of the histone methyltransferase complex polycomb repressive complex 2, is overexpressed and associated with a poor prognosis in triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC). Although EZH2 inhibition significantly alters chromatin landscapes and gene expression, it has a limited impact on the growth of TNBC models, suggesting adaptive compensatory mechanisms. In this study, we demonstrated that EZH2 inhibition causes the accumulation of misfolded proteins and double-stranded RNA, triggering an essential integrated stress response (ISR) through protein kinase R and protein kinase RNA–like endoplasmic reticulum kinase activation. By inducing ISR-mediated activating transcription factor 4 (ATF4), EZH2 inhibition enhanced amino acid flux and promoted glutaminolysis to support TNBC cell survival. Pharmacologic targeting of this metabolic axis with a glutaminase inhibitor in combination with EZH2 inhibition significantly impaired TNBC cell proliferation and tumor growth. These findings reveal a stress-driven metabolic adaptation that sustains TNBC survival upon EZH2 blockade and highlight the inhibition of this pathway as a strategy to enhance the efficacy of EZH2 inhibitors in TNBC. Significance: By inducing integrated stress response–ATF4-mediated metabolic rewiring, EZH2 inhibition creates a critical glutamine dependency in triple-negative breast cancer, exposing an actionable vulnerability through co-inhibition of glutaminase.

papers.abstract: Purpose Stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT) is standard of care for inoperable stage I or II non–small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). KEYNOTE-867 (ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT03924869 ) evaluated the addition of pembrolizumab to SBRT in participants diagnosed with stage I or II NSCLC that was inoperable or in participants who refused surgery. Methods Adults with untreated, stage I or II (T1 to limited T3, N0, M0) NSCLC (AJCC 8 th edition) that was inoperable, or adults who refused surgery, were randomly assigned 1:1 to thoracic SBRT to primary tumors for ≤2 weeks concomitantly with pembrolizumab 200 mg or placebo once every 3 weeks for ≤17 cycles. The primary end point was event-free survival (EFS) by blinded independent central review. Results A total of 448 participants were randomly assigned to SBRT plus pembrolizumab (n = 227) or SBRT plus placebo (n = 221). The median time from random assignment to the data cutoff date (June 11, 2024) for the prespecified first interim analysis was 20.6 (range, 1.3-56.8) months. The median EFS (95% CI) was 31.2 (22.5 to 39.1) months and 28.3 (19.8 to 33.1) months for the pembrolizumab and placebo arms, respectively (hazard ratio, 0.92 [95% CI, 0.69 to 1.24]; P = .2932). Among participants who received ≥1 dose of study treatment, grade 3-5 treatment-related adverse events (AEs) occurred in 46/226 (20.4%) participants in the pembrolizumab arm and 8/218 (3.7%) participants in the placebo arm. There were five treatment-related deaths all of which occurred in the pembrolizumab arm (2.2%). Conclusion The addition of pembrolizumab to SBRT did not improve EFS and was associated with a higher incidence of treatment-related AEs compared with SBRT alone in participants with inoperable stage I or II NSCLC. Based on the benefit-risk profile, the KEYNOTE-867 trial was prematurely stopped, and all study treatment was discontinued.

papers.abstract: Purpose Metastatic uveal melanoma (mUM) has poor prognosis with limited therapies. GNAQ/11 mutations that activate protein kinase C (PKC) are detected in 95% of UM tumors. Darovasertib is a first-in-class, oral, targeted PKC inhibitor that, in combination with the MET inhibitor crizotinib, has shown responses and encouraging survival outcomes in early mUM clinical trials. Here, we present phase 2 results in first-line patients with mUM treated with darovasertib 300 mg twice a day and crizotinib 200 mg twice a day. Methods The OptimUM-01 study was a phase I/II, multicenter, open-label, dose escalation and expansion study of darovasertib in patients with solid tumors harboring GNAQ/11 mutations irrespective of human leukocyte antigen status; this analysis focuses on the phase II expansion in previously untreated patients with mUM. Eligibility criteria included Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors v1.1 measurable disease, Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status 0-1, and adequate organ function. Study end points included safety, objective response rate (ORR), duration of response (DOR), disease control rate (DCR), progression-free survival (PFS), and overall survival (OS). Results Overall, 44 treatment-naïve patients were enrolled. The most common adverse events (AEs) were diarrhea (95.2%), nausea (84.1%), peripheral edema (61.4%), and vomiting (52.3%). The most common grade 3 or greater AEs were pulmonary embolism (9.1%) and iron deficiency anemia (6.8%). AEs leading to discontinuation occurred in three patients (6.8%). ORR was 34.1%, DOR was 9.0 months, and DCR was 90.2% at 8 weeks. The median PFS and OS were 7.0 months (95% CI, 5.0 to 8.3) and 21.1 months (95% CI, 11.9 to 20.7), respectively. Conclusion Results from OptimUM-01 suggest that the combination of darovasertib and crizotinib has encouraging efficacy with a manageable safety profile and may represent a first-in-class targeted treatment option for patients with previously untreated mUM.

papers.abstract: Background: Prehabilitation is recommended to reduce surgery-related functional decline but is not routinely integrated into presurgical breast cancer care, often resulting in rehabilitation being delayed until after surgery. We conducted a retrospective comparative effectiveness study evaluating outcomes associated with real-world prehabilitation versus delayed rehabilitation care models. Methods: Women who began rehabilitation before (prehabilitation; n=416) or after breast cancer surgery (delayed rehabilitation; n=232) were identified from the electronic medical record. Upper extremity function and health-related quality of life (HRQoL) outcomes were extracted presurgery, postsurgery, and at final evaluation. Adjusted linear mixed-effect models examined change over time and between-group differences, and logistic regression estimated likelihood of achieving normal limits. Analyses were conducted overall and stratified by surgery type. Rehabilitation utilization and recovery to baseline levels among patients who received prehabilitation were summarized descriptively. Results: Prehabilitation was associated with superior postsurgery function and HRQoL, as well as higher odds of achieving normal limits, compared with delayed rehabilitation. Both groups improved during postoperative rehabilitation; however, functional outcomes and strength remained superior among patients who received prehabilitation at final evaluation. Benefits of prehabilitation were most pronounced among women undergoing mastectomy or bilateral mastectomy, although meaningful benefits were also observed following lumpectomy. All patients who received prehabilitation recovered to baseline levels on at least one outcome. Across the perioperative period, patients who received prehabilitation attended fewer visits than those who received delayed rehabilitation (median, 5 vs 7; P =.008). Conclusions: Both prehabilitation and delayed rehabilitation supported recovery of upper extremity functioning and HRQoL following breast cancer surgery. However, prehabilitation may represent a more effective and efficient care model—particularly for women undergoing more extensive surgical procedures—achieving comparable or better outcomes with fewer visits. These findings support integration of prehabilitation into breast cancer surgical care pathways.

papers.abstract: Abstract Histone lactylation is an epigenetic modification that connects lactate metabolism with protein function. Our study identified that lactate enhances the protein lactylation level not only in the myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSC) of tumor-bearing mice but also in the tumor tissues of patients with lung cancer. This modification led to the upregulation of CD38 expression and enhanced the immunosuppressive function of MDSCs. Mechanistically, CD38 promoted immunosuppression by depleting NAD+, and treatment with a CD38 inhibitor or siRNA-mediated knockdown of CD38 in MDSCs delayed tumor progression. Histone H3 lysine 18 is enriched at the CD38 promoter region, with p300, histone deacetylases 1 to 3, and bromodomain-containing protein 4 identified as key epigenetic regulators in this process. Our findings reveal the critical role of the lactate–CD38–NAD+ axis in regulating MDSC immunosuppressive function and establish histone lactylation as an epigenetic mechanism controlling CD38 expression.

papers.abstract: Abstract The spatial arrangement of immune cells in the tumor microenvironment (TME) varies widely, from dispersed to clustered and tumor-excluded to infiltrating. Multiplexed spatial profiling is an effective means of characterizing tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes and immune complexes such as tertiary lymphoid structures (TLS) in the TME. However, few approaches have been described for objectively parametrizing patterns of immune organization and assessing their association with biological or clinical variables. This makes it difficult to evaluate whether a set of tumors is relatively immunologically cold or hot. In this study, we describe an intuitive set of statistical tools (available in the R package, tlsR) for characterizing lymphocyte patterns in the TME of solid cancers. We applied tlsR to primary prostate cancer, which is often described as immunologically “cold.” Using a cohort of 29 radical prostatectomy specimens stratified into low Gleason grade (LGG; n = 15) and high Gleason grade (HGG; n = 14), we showed that HGG prostate cancer is significantly more infiltrated than LGG prostate cancer, with lymphocytes organized into B or T cell–enriched immune clusters (IC). A subset of these ICs had the B- and T-cell zonation and follicular dendritic cells characteristic of bona fide TLSs. HGGs were also enriched with ICs containing precursors of exhausted T cells and proliferating B cells, and their tumor compartments harbored granzyme B+ cytotoxic T cells in contact with cancer cells. Thus, far from being cold, a subset of HGG prostate cancer has features associated with active immune surveillance, a finding with implications for emerging prostate cancer immunotherapies.

papers.abstract: Activated Cdc42-associated kinase 1 (ACK1; encoded by the TNK2 gene) is an oncogenic protein of the non-receptor tyrosine kinase family and functions downstream of RAS and activated transmembrane receptor tyrosine kinases such as EGFR. Non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), which constitutes around 85% of lung cancer cases, often exhibits amplification or overexpression of the TNK2 gene. This study focuses on demonstrating the therapeutic potential of targeting ACK1 for the treatment of NSCLC. The small molecule ACK1 inhibitor, (R)-9b, preferentially inhibited the growth of NSCLC cell lines possessing activated ACK1, which often have RAS mutations. (R)-9b induced G2/M arrest and robust cellular senescence primarily in the sensitive RAS mutant NSCLC cell lines; these effects were confirmed with ACK1 knockdown. (R)-9b significantly inhibited the growth of both cell line-derived and patient-derived NSCLC xenografts with RAS mutations in vivo. Mechanistically, ACK1 inhibition suppresses topoisomerase 2A (Topo IIα; encoded by TOP2A) expression, along with downregulation of the expression of gene sets associated with the regulation of DNA repair and replication, resulting in accumulation of DNA damage and subsequent cellular senescence. Overall, RAS mutation in NSCLC cell lines activates the Cdc42/ACK1 axis, conferring sensitivity to ACK1 inhibition that causes accumulation of DNA damage via inhibition of Topo IIα and DNA repair, G2/M arrest, and eventual cellular senescence in RAS mutant NSCLC cells.

papers.abstract: Abstract Background Edematous malnutrition, aka kwashiorkor, is a phenotype of severe malnutrition whose pathophysiology remains poorly understood. Methods In this case-control study, we employed plasma lipidomics, metabolomics, and proteomics, urine metabolomics and gut microbiome profiling to delineate molecular features specific to kwashiorkor in 60 children aged 6–59 months from Niger compared to marasmus ( n = 60) and non-malnourished children (NAM) ( n = 60) matched by age, sex, and clinical triage score. Features were defined as kwashiorkor-specific if they also correlated with edema severity and normalized following nutritional rehabilitation. Results We identified a plasma proteomic factor featuring lumican, gelsolin, and tetranectin and a lipidomic factor enriched in sphingolipids. Both differed in kwashiorkor compared to marasmus and NAM, were associated with edema grade, and trended towards normalcy after nutritional treatment, which are consistent with ECM remodeling and sphingolipid dysregulation. In contrast, neither (plasma and urine) metabolomic profiles nor gut microbiome composition showed kwashiorkor-specific signatures, although our urine and gut microbiome analyses may be underpowered. Conclusion These findings advance understanding of kwashiorkor pathophysiology beyond nutrient deficiency and highlight ECM and sphingolipid features associated with its distinct clinical and molecular characteristics compared to marasmus.

papers.abstract: Timdarpacept (IMM01) is a recombinant signal regulatory protein α-IgG1 fusion protein that exerts antitumor activity by blocking the "don't eat me" signal while simultaneously activating the "eat me" signal, inducing robust antibody-dependent cellular phagocytosis. We report the final phase II results of treatment-naïve higher risk chronic myelomonocytic leukemia (CMML) patients treated with IMM01 in combination with azacitidine. We assessed the safety and efficacy of IMM01 in combination with azacitidine (AZA) as first-line therapy for newly diagnosed CMML patients. IMM01 was administered intravenously at 2.0 mg/kg weekly, and AZA was administered subcutaneously at 75 mg/m² on days 1-7 of each 28-day cycle. As of the data cut-off on May 13, 2025, 24 patients were enrolled. Of 22 efficacy-evaluable patients, the overall response rate (ORR) was 72.7% (16/22; 95% CI 49.8-89.3), including 27.3% complete response (CR), 13.6% marrow CR (mCR) with hematologic improvement (HI), 4.5% HI alone, and 27.3% mCR alone. The median time to response was 1.8 months (range, 0.9-3.6), and the median duration of response was 16.9 months (95% CI 5.1-NE). Median overall survival and progression-free survival were 22.2 months (95% CI 9.0-NE) and 17.8 months (95% CI 5.3-NE), respectively. The most common grade ≥ 3 treatment-related adverse events (≥ 10%) were lymphopenia (66.7%), leukopenia (62.5%), neutropenia (62.5%), thrombocytopenia (58.3%), anemia (33.3%), and pneumonia (16.7%). IMM01 in combination with AZA was generally well tolerated and effective in treatment-naïve higher risk CMML patients. Trial registration ClinicalTrials.gov identiﬁer: NCT05140811.

papers.abstract: Familial hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (FHLH) is classically pediatric, but adult-onset disease is increasingly recognized. Whether adult-onset FHLH differs from pediatric/adolescent-onset disease remains incompletely defined. We aimed to characterize age-related differences in a nationwide multicenter cohort of patients with FHLH in China. We conducted a nationwide multicenter retrospective study of 223 patients with FHLH from 27 centers in China. Genetic architecture, central nervous system (CNS) involvement, allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (allo-HSCT), and survival were compared by age at onset, with adult-onset disease defined as onset at age ≥ 18 years and pediatric/adolescent-onset disease as onset at < 18 years. In this cohort, adult-onset disease accounted for 54/223 cases (24.2%). In the PRF1/UNC13D subset (n = 192), higher non-truncating variant burden was associated with adult onset (unadjusted OR per additional recorded variant, 1.95; 95% CI, 1.17-3.39), although the association attenuated after adjustment for gene and zygosity (adjusted OR, 1.58; 95% CI, 0.94-2.75). Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) was the predominant documented trigger in adults. CNS involvement was common across age groups (46.4%), with uncertain prognostic significance. Adults underwent allo-HSCT less frequently (49.1% vs. 70.2%) and were less often in complete response before transplantation (15.4% vs. 46.8%). Adult onset remained associated with poorer overall survival after multivariable adjustment including time-dependent allo-HSCT (HR, 3.74; 95% CI, 1.96-7.12). Post-HSCT survival was also poorer in adults. Adult-onset FHLH was associated with non-truncating variant enrichment and poorer overall and post-HSCT survival. These findings support considering inherited disease despite acquired triggers and careful assessment of disease control and transplant-related risks in adults with FHLH.
